newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean chipmakers' profit seen rising sharply.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean chipmakers' profit seen rising sharply.

text.p: A recent recovery in memory chip prices is expected to continue through this year, sharply raising profits of South Korean chipmakers, company officials and analysts said on Tuesday.
"I expect some companies to see their net profit more than double this year as prices and productivity are improving," said Tony Jung, an analyst at Jardine Fleming Securities.
Officials at Samsung Electronics Co, LG Semicon Co and Hyundai Electronics Industries Co said they expected their net profits to improve.

The per-unit spot price for 16-megabit dynamic random access memory (DRAM) chips -- the brains of most of today's personal computers -- was now hovering at $10-$12, up from about $6 late last year, they said.
Production cutbacks by South Korean makers and moves by Japanese makers to scrap major capacity expansion plans since late last year led the recovery in prices, they said.
Excess global supplies of DRAMs caused prices to fall more than 80 percent last year, and South Korea's three chipmakers saw their net profits plunge about 90 percent as a result.

Samsung's net profit fell to 164.2 billion won ($183.4 million) in 1996 from 2.5 trillion in 1995. The net profit of Hyundai and LG fell to 71.1 billion won and 91.1 billion won, respectively, from 834.6 billion and 778.5 billion in 1995.
A Samsung spokesman said he expected DRAM prices to rise further to $13-$14 on average in the second quarter before easing slightly the following quarter.
"We see the unit price possibly going up to as high as $15 during the period, with the average at between $13 and $14," Samsung spokesman Yoon Jong-jin told Reuters.
Yoon said the price was expected to pick up again in the fourth quarter, traditionally the peak season for personal computer sales in the United States.
Growing sales of memory-hungry personal computers with stronger multimedia capabilities were also cited as supporting demand for DRAMs.
For example, computers with Intel Corp's MMX processors require 32 megabits of RAM, compared with eight to 16 megabits for conventional models, analysts said.
LG Semicon spokesman Lee Baek-soo said he also was optimistic about this year's price recovery and an improvement in the company's annual profit.
But analysts said a surge in supplies by Taiwan makers, expected from July, could pressure the global prices.
"I am sceptical on whether this could be sustained, and see the supply of Taiwanese products as a major variable," said Jang Yun-yong, an analyst at Hyundai Securities.
Taiwan makers are estimated to account for between six and 15 percent of world supplies of 16-megabit DRAMs.
But Jardine's Jung said South Korean makers were well ahead of Taiwan both in productivity and production technology.
